A.explanation: 2 V is only the p.d. across the $2R$ resistor, not the full p.d. across the $3R + 2R + R$ series branch.

B.explanation: 4 V would ignore the $3\text{ V}$ across $3R$ and $1\text{ V}$ across $R$ that are in series with the $2R$ resistor.

C.explanation: Current in the series branch is $I = 2/(2R)$, giving $3\text{ V} + 2\text{ V} + 1\text{ V} = 6\text{ V}$ across the battery.

D.explanation: 10 V is the sum $R+2R+3R+4R$ treated as one series chain, but $4R$ is in parallel with the battery, not in series.

hints: Notice the voltmeter is connected directly across only the $2R$ resistor, where it reads $2\text{ V}$.
Trace the right-hand loop: $3R$, $2R$ and $R$ are in series with each other, and that whole series combination is in parallel with the battery and with $4R$.
Find the common current in $3R$, $2R$ and $R$ from $I = V/R$ for the $2R$ resistor, then add the three $IR$ drops to get the battery p.d.
walkthrough: Identify the two parallel branches across the battery: one branch is $4R$ alone, the other branch is $3R$, $2R$ and $R$ in series.
In the series branch the same current $I$ flows through all three resistors. Use the $2R$ resistor where the p.d. is known: $I = V_{2R}/(2R) = 2/(2R) = 1/R$.
Calculate the other series p.d.s with $V = IR$: $V_{3R} = I \times 3R = 3\text{ V}$ and $V_{R} = I \times R = 1\text{ V}$.
Add p.d.s around the series branch: $V_{branch} = 3\text{ V} + 2\text{ V} + 1\text{ V} = 6\text{ V}$.
The battery has negligible internal resistance, so its e.m.f. equals the terminal p.d. across either parallel branch, which is $6\text{ V}$. This is option C
